title: Default arguments are initialized once when a function is created.
body: Python's default arguments are not values that are created anew each time a function is called. They are initialized once when the function is defined and can be reused in subsequent calls. Therefore, you should be especially careful when reading the default values of lists and dictionaries.
detail: Values that don’t change, such as numbers or strings, rarely cause major problems. However, if you use a value whose contents can change—such as a list or a dict—as a default argument, changes made in a previous call may carry over to the next call. Therefore, you must carefully distinguish whether a default argument is simply a default value or a value that can share state between calls.

title: The default value of a list can be shared
body: If you pass a list directly as the default argument, it may appear as though the same list is being reused when the function is called multiple times. Therefore, if you assume that a new empty list is created each time the function is called, you may misinterpret the results.
detail: Beginners often assume, “Since the function was called again, it will start with an empty list.” However, if the default `list` is reused, the values appended during the first call remain in the result of the second call, leading to unexpected output. This issue becomes a harder-to-find bug in projects with multiple functions intertwined than in code that is short.

title: Pass "None" as an argument and create a new list inside the function
body: If you need to change the default value, set the default argument to `None` and use a pattern where you create a new list or dictionary inside the function. This approach helps reduce the problem of values being shared surreptitiously between calls.
detail: If you start with `def f(items=None):` and then handle it with `if items is None: items = []`, you can create a new list each time the function is called, if necessary. This helps reduce the problem of values from previous calls being mixed into subsequent calls. This pattern is frequently used not only with lists but also when handling mutable default values such as dictionaries and sets.

title: Changing a value within a function can affect the subsequent flow of the program.
body: Operations within a function that modify existing objects—such as `list.append`—can affect the state outside the function or the results of subsequent calls. Therefore, you should check not only the function’s return value but also whether the object has been modified.
detail: This kind of change can be called a side effect. Beginners tend to focus only on the return value, but in reality, they also need to check whether the original list has been modified within the function. This can lead to confusing bugs, especially when combined with default arguments. Therefore, for operations that modify existing objects—such as `append`, `update`, and `pop`—it’s important to get into the habit of checking the state of the object both before and after the function call.
